newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa defends pharmaceutical policy changes.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa defends pharmaceutical policy changes.

text.p: South Africa's state health department on Tuesday defended controversial planned changes to pharmaceutical policy, saying the aim was to cut the price of medicines which had soared in the apartheid era.
Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma has introduced a bill which would among other things promote the use of cheaper generic medicines at the expense of branded drugs.
The government would no longer buy branded drugs, and pharmacists would in most cases be obliged to tell customers with prescriptions for them that the generic version was cheaper.

The bill would also allow "parallel" imports, clearing the way for medicines not registered in South Africa to be brought in from abroad as long as their components are identical to drugs that are registered.
Olive Shishana, director general of the health department, told a parliamentary committee on health policy that criticism of the changes, mainly from the pharmaceutical industry, was misplaced.
"South Africa is unique in buying (medicines) nationally," she said, citing the example of the European Union whose members on average import 60 percent of their pharmaceuticals.
"Prices are so high here because apartheid isolated this country to the point where we tried to depend on ourselves for everything."
Shishana said the main focus of the legislation was to make health care affordable.
"Parallel import simply means we buy the same product, from the same manufacturer, but at a lower price," she said.
"(This) policy will only be implemented if the pharmaceutical industry in this country does not give us cheaper prices...

"It will let the market forces work. You simply include the international companies on the scene. You simply include other countries, it's real competition," Shishana said. "We are not going to bring in back-door medicine that has not been properly evaluated."
Ian Roberts, a special adviser to the health department, told the committee that generic medicines were just as good and just as safe as branded ones.
Roberts said that under the present system doctors training in the state service became "branded" to drugs and continued prescribing them in private practice.
He said the pharmaceutical industry feared that once the government started buying only generic medicines, manufacturers would lose this source of promotion for their products.
